findings.claim: the conflict-resolution chapter distinguishes five decision-making modes for handling disagreements (Ch 14)
findings.failure_mode: concept re-labelled and attributed to the chapter
findings.evidence: Deep 440-448: Thomas's five conflict-resolution modes (Ch 14.2, Exhibit 14.4). Source 21166: 'Thomas has identified five modes for conflict resolution'. The chapter does not call them decision-making modes; line 151 frames that reading as the distillation's own, which is fine.
findings.fix: correct: the conflict chapter distinguishes Thomas's five conflict-resolution modes (Ch 14.2), and choosing among them is itself a decision

findings.claim: The reactive route is appropriate when experience teaches the right response and speed matters
findings.failure_mode: source-supported, absent from deep
findings.evidence: Deep 173 gives only 'strong emotions pull ... toward the reactive route; novel and complex situations call for the reflective route'. Source 8127-8136 (experienced managers decide quickly because experience taught them; the quick route can be lifesaving) and 9077-9079 ('the reactive system can be lifesaving when time is of the essence, and it can be much more efficient when based on developed experience and expertise') carry the claim.
findings.fix: cycle-to-deep: add to deep Part VI 'Two-system processing': the reactive route 'can be lifesaving when time is of the essence' and is efficient 'when based on developed experience and expertise' (Ch 6.2; source 8127-8136, 9077-9079).

findings.claim: ... including external evidence about stakeholders, contextual factors, costs, benefits ... This approach is particularly valuable for new managers and for experienced managers starting something new.
findings.failure_mode: source-supported, absent from deep
findings.evidence: Deep 196 says only that EBDM means 'systematically collecting the best available evidence rather than relying on intuition'. Source 8614-8621 carries the external-evidence list and 'particularly beneficial for new managers or for experienced managers who are starting something new'.
findings.fix: cycle-to-deep: add source 8614-8621 (Ch 6.5, 'Do you have the best-quality data and evidence?') to deep Part VI 'Improving decision quality'.

findings.claim: Critical thinking ... A disciplined process of evaluating information quality and arguments.
findings.failure_mode: source-supported, absent from deep
findings.evidence: Deep 196 gives no definition, only that critical thinking requires recognising fallacies. Source 8640-8642: 'Critical thinking is a disciplined process of evaluating the quality of information, especially data collected from other sources and arguments made by other people'.
findings.fix: cycle-to-deep: add the Ch 6.5 definition (source 8640-8642) to deep Part VI.

findings.claim: Moral sensitivity (recognising the issue has a moral component), moral judgment (determining right versus wrong), moral motivation/intention (deciding to do the right thing), moral character/action (actually doing it).
findings.failure_mode: source-supported, absent from deep
findings.evidence: Deep 198 names the four components without glosses. Source 8749-8752 gives exactly these glosses.
findings.fix: cycle-to-deep: add the component glosses (source 8749-8752, Ch 6.5) to deep 198.

findings.claim: Cognitive complexity is partly trait, partly cultivable through structured habits.
findings.failure_mode: claim not in deep or source
findings.evidence: Deep 47 calls cognitive complexity 'a central managerial trait'. Source 1959-2010 (Ch 2.2) describes low- and high-complexity characteristics and their effects on leadership and decisions; it says nothing about cultivating it.
findings.fix: strip

findings.claim: The implication for decision-making is that the *process* matters as much as the outcome — procedural justice can sustain commitment even when distributive outcomes disappoint.
findings.failure_mode: mechanism not in deep
findings.evidence: Deep 239 [AP] (Ch 7.4) defines distributive and procedural justice and gives the seniority-layoff example only. Source 11128-11147 says nothing about commitment or about process mattering as much as outcome. Same finding as the software-business audit (D007, D015, D022).
findings.fix: correct: The implication for decision-making is that people judge both the outcome (distributive justice) and the process used to reach it (procedural justice); layoffs based on seniority are seen as fairer than layoffs based on supervisors' opinions (Ch 7.4).

findings.claim: Where are the deontological lines?
findings.failure_mode: vocabulary imported from outside the source
findings.evidence: grep 'deontolog' in the converted source: 0 hits; the deep carries only Rest's four-component model (deep 198). The question's premise (some options are ruled out on ethical grounds) is supported; the ethical-theory label is not the source's.
findings.fix: correct: Where are the lines I will not cross, however good the option looks on other criteria?

findings.claim: Have I generated three to five real alternatives, not just one or two? The text observes that managers often stop at two and pick the better.
findings.failure_mode: invented count; source observation absent from deep
findings.evidence: Deep 179: 'generate alternatives' is step 2, with no count. Source 8567-8571 (Ch 6.5, 'Step 2'): managers often generate two alternatives 'and then quickly moves to Step 3 in order to make a quick decision'; 'Generating many possible options will increase the likelihood of reaching a good decision.' 'Three to five' is in neither; 'pick the better' loosens 'quickly moves to Step 3'. Same pattern as software-business D013.
findings.fix: correct: Have I generated many real alternatives, not just two? The text observes that managers often generate two and move straight to analysis. cycle-to-deep: source 8567-8571.

findings.claim: Have I given my mind permission to wander, combine ideas in novel ways, or step back from the traditional framing?
findings.failure_mode: source-supported, absent from deep
findings.evidence: Deep Part VI has no creativity content. Source 8589-8600 (Ch 6.5, 'Be creative'): creativity 'requires ... the ability to step back from traditional ways of doing things' and 'letting your mind wander and combining existing knowledge from past experiences in novel ways'.
findings.fix: cycle-to-deep: add source 8589-8600 (Ch 6.5, 'Be creative') to deep Part VI.

findings.claim: If this decision were on the front page of a major newspaper tomorrow, would I feel guilty or proud? Which feeling is the decision-relevant signal?
findings.failure_mode: source-supported, absent from deep
findings.evidence: Deep 198 carries Rest's model but not the newspaper test. Source 8762-8765: 'think about how you would feel if that decision ended up on the front page of a major newspaper. If you would feel guilty or ashamed, don't do it! Pay attention to those emotional cues'.
findings.fix: cycle-to-deep: add the front-page test (source 8762-8765, Ch 6.5, moral judgment) to deep 198.

findings.claim: Follow-up: name the ethical dimension; consider the news-test ("how would this look on the front page")
findings.failure_mode: source-supported, absent from deep (recurrence of D011)
findings.evidence: As D011: source 8762-8765; the source places the test under moral judgment (component 2), not moral sensitivity.
findings.fix: cycle-to-deep: as D011.

findings.claim: This worked example illustrates several key concepts in the source: ... escalation precommitment ...
findings.failure_mode: example's own design move listed as a source concept
findings.evidence: Deep 186 defines escalation of commitment; no precommitment remedy appears in the deep. Source 8317-8325 says effective managers 'are willing to reevaluate decisions and change direction when appropriate'; nothing on precommitment.
findings.fix: correct: replace 'escalation precommitment' with 'escalation of commitment (countered here by the example's own precommitment device)'.

findings.claim: Conflict-avoidance leading to compounding problems. Avoiding process conflict prevents productive exploration; avoiding relationship conflict allows poor performance to continue.
findings.failure_mode: source's advice inverted for relationship conflict
findings.evidence: Deep 192 and source 8418-8420: relationship conflict 'is generally harmful and should be quelled when possible'; source 8424-8425 tells managers to keep feedback on 'behaviors and activities (how things are done) rather than on the individual' to avoid it. The poor-performance case (source 8386-8414, the late employee) is about not avoiding a necessary corrective conversation, not about engaging relationship conflict.
findings.fix: correct: Avoiding process conflict prevents productive exploration; avoiding a necessary corrective conversation lets poor performance continue (Ch 6.4). Keep that conversation on behaviours so it does not become relationship conflict.

findings.claim: Equity theory predicts disengagement when the link between effort, performance, and reward is unclear; expectancy theory predicts the same.
findings.failure_mode: one theory's mechanism given to another
findings.evidence: Deep 231: equity theory compares one's outcome-input ratio with a referent's. Deep 233: the effort-performance-outcome link is expectancy theory's. Same finding as software-business D032.
findings.fix: correct: Expectancy theory predicts weaker motivation when the link between effort, performance and reward is unclear; equity theory adds that people who see their outcome-input ratio as unfair against a referent act to restore balance, including by leaving. (Source: Ch 7.3)

findings.claim: Practitioners working in decision-making contexts should treat Simon's framing as the explanation for why the six-step process and evidence-based methods exist.
findings.failure_mode: rationale not in deep
findings.evidence: Deep 179 and 196 present the six-step process and EBDM as ways to improve decision quality; deep 183-190 set them against six barriers, not bounded rationality alone. No passage calls bounded rationality the reason they exist.
findings.fix: correct: The text sets the six-step process and evidence-based methods against the barriers of Ch 6.4, bounded rationality first among them.

findings.claim: ... and that escalation of commitment is one of those resolutions.
findings.failure_mode: link not in deep or source
findings.evidence: Deep 87 (Ch 3.4, 'Behavioral Justification'): tension resolved by changing behaviour or attitude. Deep 186 (Ch 6.4) defines escalation of commitment. Neither links them; source 4063-4075 and 8317-8325 do not either.
findings.fix: strip: end the row at '... through behaviour change or attitude change.'

findings.claim: Goal theory and decision-making are paired: difficult, specific, accepted goals shape what decisions get made and which alternatives feel salient.
findings.failure_mode: mechanism not in deep
findings.evidence: Deep 232: goal theory says difficult, specific, accepted goals produce better performance; it lists hazards (goal conflict, narrow goals neglecting other duties, over-emphasis on quantifiable measures). Nothing pairs goal theory with decision-making or says goals shape which alternatives feel salient.
findings.fix: correct: Goal theory (Ch 7.3): difficult, specific, accepted goals improve performance, but narrow or over-quantified goals can crowd out other duties, a hazard to weigh when a decision sets targets.

findings.claim: ... offers a bottom-up alternative to top-down systematic decision-making and may produce stronger commitment to the resulting decision.
findings.failure_mode: hedged extrapolation not in deep
findings.evidence: Deep 536 and 725: AI is abundance-based and bottom-up; 'the more complex the potential change, the greater the need to involve employees'. Source 24819-24909 says appreciative conversations shift narratives and 'inspire a shift in the actions that employees initiate'; no claim about commitment.
findings.fix: correct: ... offers a bottom-up alternative that has employees co-create the vision and design the actions (Ch 16.3).

findings.claim: Leon Festinger, cognitive dissonance — mentioned in Ch 3.4 without explicit naming; cited in the deep ref as influencing escalation-of-commitment analysis [BT].
findings.failure_mode: claim about the deep ref that the deep ref does not hold
findings.evidence: Deep 87 and 696: Festinger's cognitive dissonance 'mentioned without explicit naming' (Ch 3.4). No mention of escalation of commitment.
findings.fix: correct: Leon Festinger, cognitive dissonance — mentioned in Ch 3.4 without explicit naming [BT].

findings.claim: Thomas-Kilmann conflict modes
findings.failure_mode: co-author name not in deep or source
findings.evidence: Deep 438-448 and source 21136-21244 attribute the model to Kenneth W. Thomas only; grep 'Kilmann' in the converted source: 0 hits.
findings.fix: correct: Kenneth Thomas's conflict-resolution modes

findings.claim: Chris Argyris, basic incongruity thesis — organisation-vs-maturity conflict underlying participatory management arguments (Ch 2.5) [BT].
findings.failure_mode: link not in deep
findings.evidence: Deep 55 and 691: Argyris anchors the personality-organisation conflict treatment; strongest at lower levels. Neither the deep nor source 2309-2380 ties it to participatory management arguments.
findings.fix: correct: organisation-vs-maturity conflict, strongest in highly structured, mechanised lower-level jobs (Ch 2.5) [BT].

findings.claim: The cross-cultural negotiation section draws on decades-old American/Arab/Russian typologies (Table 14.5)
findings.failure_mode: source-supported, absent from deep
findings.evidence: Deep 466 gives no date. Source 21806 ('North America, the Middle East, and the former Soviet Union') and endnote 31845-31846 (Glenn, Witmeyer and Stevenson, 'Cultural Styles of Persuasion', 1977) support 'decades-old'.
findings.fix: cycle-to-deep: add to deep 466 that Table 14.5 draws on Glenn, Witmeyer and Stevenson (1977).

findings.claim: Key Concepts 1–10 are `[AP]` or `[AE]` drawn from the source.
findings.failure_mode: marker claim not borne out by the file or the deep
findings.evidence: Key Concepts 1-10 carry no [AP] or [AE] markers; their only markers are four [V] quotations (lines 16, 22, 28, 30). The deep passages they paraphrase are marked [AP], [AR], [BT] or [V]; none is [AE].

notes: Counting: claims_audited counts distinct assertions (relevance sentences, key-concept sub-claims, table rows, pattern and anti-pattern items, worked-example steps, integration rows, borrowed-through items, named limits, integrity-note items); faithful = claims_audited - findings. Quote check against the converted source: 'the brain can only use one system at a time for processing information' (8122-8123), 'can actually lead to improved performance' (8416-8417), Rest's 'a failure at any point in the chain can lead to unethical actions' (8755) and the groupthink definition (8906-8908) are word for word. The derived-from-deep sha256 (a475cbbb...) matches the current deep ref. Structural (not graded): the Integration section lists six frameworks inside this same source (Simon, Festinger, Locke, Vroom, Thomas, Cooperrider) and links to no other corpus reference, which the protocol's Integration template requires; the Worked Example carries no verbatim blockquote. Recurring claim listed at each occurrence: newspaper test (D011, D012). Applied guidance judged faithful: the Phase 1-6 questions other than those listed, the 'perfection is unattainable' row (bounded rationality, deep 185), the bad-luck-vs-bad-decision row (uncertainty, deep 188), the similarity-bias framing of loyalty in the Worked Example (source 8343-8352 counts shared experiences as a similarity basis), and the milestone conversation as process conflict (source 8424-8425: keep feedback on how things are done). Deep-ref gaps surfaced (cycling candidates): source 8127-8136 and 9077-9079 (reactive route and experience), 8567-8571 (managers stop at two alternatives), 8589-8600 (creativity), 8614-8621 (EBDM detail), 8640-8642 (critical-thinking definition), 8749-8752 and 8762-8765 (Rest glosses, front-page test), 31845-31846 (Table 14.5 dated 1977). Deep-ref error surfaced: deep 688 says bounded rationality (Simon) is 'cited as foundational' at Ch 6.4, but the source's Ch 6.4 'Bounded Rationality' subsection (8286-8298) never names Simon; Simon appears only in the Dearborn-Simon study (Ch 3.1) and the Ch 13.2 decision-criteria quote (19855). The distillation's Simon attributions (lines 147, 158) follow the deep and are graded against it.
